papers.title: How Effective Is (More) Money? Randomizing Unconditional Cash Transfer Amounts in the US

human_issues.text: The paper's discussion of mechanisms by which attrition could bias results (Section C.4) does not address unobservable mechanisms; the evaluator notes many remain possible, so concerns are only partly allayed.
human_issues.quote: There remain many additional possible mechanisms based on unobservables, but the evidence presented in this section helps to allay concerns about some of the more straightforward possibilities

human_issues.text: The mediation analysis is limited to controlling for mediators and observing how treatment effects change. The evaluator considers this the most important improvement needed and points to alternative approaches such as Acharya, Blackwell, and Sen (2016).
human_issues.quote: Most importantly, the mediation analysis can improve beyond just controlling for mediators and checking how the mani effects change.

human_issues.text: The mediators are aggregated; the evaluator suggests disaggregating them (Money Mind—Cost, Overwhelmed by Others' Needs, Spending Stress) and testing each separately in Table H.11 to see whether treatment effects change.
human_issues.quote: The mediators can be further disaggregated; the variables, Money Mind -- Cost, Overwhelmed Others' Needs, and Spending Stress can be used in Table H.11 separately

human_issues.text: The evaluator asks whether heterogeneous treatment effects were examined by prior income level, arguing that effects may depend on where participants sit in the income distribution or on transfer size relative to income.
human_issues.quote: Did the authors try exploring het[erogeneous] effects according to the previous level of income?

model_issues.text: Differential attrition (Control 80% vs cash 88–90%): Lee bounds include meaningful positive effects, and modest missing-data gaps (0.18–0.46 SD) would erase the negative point estimates, so 'cash made people feel worse' is fragile.

Experimenter demand / strategic reporting is not ruled out. Bank data show cash recipients underreported income and savings more than Control post-treatment, which undermines interpreting subjective declines as true welfare losses.

Mechanism evidence is non-preregistered correlational mediation using post-treatment mediators (spending stress, overwhelmed by others' needs, money on the mind) that overlap conceptually with or are components of the outcomes.
The objective vs subjective split is post hoc, with few objective items. Some objective items (earned income, housing debt) also move negatively.
Treatment-on-treated and complete-responder restrictions attenuate effects toward zero, consistent with selection contributing to the negative estimates.

The model is an uncalibrated numerical illustration with an assumed misperception of shock size. It rationalizes rather than tests the result, and the lack of a $500 vs $2,000 difference is not well explained.

The strategic-responding sub-experiment uses a weak manipulation, and the reference-dependence experiment includes holiday-confounded waves. Both sub-experiments were added mid-trial for later waves only.
External validity is limited: a COVID-era sample of nonprofit applicants, predominantly female, with concurrent stimulus checks and prior receipt of nonprofit cash.
The expert-prediction comparison relies on forecasters interpreting SD effects on composite indices. This is partly addressed by single-item predictions.
Bank data cover a self-selected 43%, and the claim that spending patterns generalize rests on similar survey results in that subsample.
Data and analysis code for the main RCT do not appear to be publicly provided; only model code is linked.

codex.reason: Both identify the mediation analysis as inadequate mechanism evidence, though A1 specifically flags post-treatment and outcome-overlapping mediators.

papers.title: A Welfare Analysis of Policies Impacting Climate Change

human_issues.text: Some policy categories, such as cap-and-trade, rest on very few studies, and this limitation is not acknowledged explicitly enough.
human_issues.quote: Some policy categories have very few studies (e.g., cap-and-trade). This limitation should be acknowledged more explicitly.

human_issues.text: The report notes the paper's cost-benefit ratio for a Pigouvian tax seems inconsistent: the pollution reduction lowers tax income equally, so the ratio is unaltered only when lambda equals u', and the presentation of this case is unclear.
human_issues.quote: As by the definition of a Pigouvian tax, the tax $\tau$ equals the externality V, the SVPF is unaltered. However for the cost-benefit ratio that is only the case for $\lambda=u'$.

model_issues.text: Learning-by-doing benefits (global experience curves treated as causal, fully external, no internal capture, perfect competition, no future subsidies) drive the residential solar and EV results (solar 1.45→3.86; EV 0.96→1.45). Appendix Table 1 undermines the robustness claim: the wind coefficient turns positive with a time trend and the solar coefficient becomes implausibly large.

Overlapping policies (binding RPS, RGGI/California caps) are not addressed: induced renewable generation or conservation may yield zero net emission reductions under binding caps or standards, potentially overstating the highest MVPFs (wind, solar, regional nudges).

Wind PTC MVPFs rely on only three US elasticity estimates from 1998–2011, extrapolated to 2020 under constant elasticity; the category CI is [2.73, ∞), and a constant semi-elasticity cuts the MVPF from 5.87 to 2.86.

Internal numerical inconsistencies: Table 2 gasoline-tax values (category 0.765; Gas (Small) 0.718; Gas (DK) 0.602) conflict with Table 3, Appendix Table 3, Figure 7 and the text (0.671, 0.605, 0.437). The abstract and conclusion also disagree on thresholds ("exceeding 2" vs "exceeding 3"; "below 0.7" vs other fuel taxes ~0.80 and CA cap-and-trade ~0.94).

Gas tax MVPFs depend heavily on accident and congestion externalities (~$1.40/gal) and exclude labor-market tax-interaction effects based on a single study; the climate-specific interpretation is therefore overstated.

Cap-and-trade estimates require strong extrapolations (constant dp/dq over time, leakage values, unobserved responses for 95% of California covered emissions), and the RGGI result is dominated by local co-benefits.

International MVPFs (e.g., Kenyan cookstoves at 37 US-only and 323 global) hinge on the fully non-renewable biomass assumption (7 vs 1.67 tCO2) and on the taxable-US-productivity share of SCC damages; the headline placement overstates precision.

Nudge MVPFs assume zero private WTP, full government financing, and counted utility profit losses; the regional results depend on AVERT marginal-emission regions (the Northwest classification is questionable).

Ad hoc valuation assumptions (Harberger 50% valuation for marginal recipients, an assumed 50% inframarginal share for weatherization, equal weighting in category averages, inclusion of possibly foreign firm profits in WTP) receive limited systematic sensitivity analysis.

The publication-bias correction is limited (mainly subsidies), and the authors' own figure shows the Andrews–Kasy model fits poorly, so the claim that conclusions are unaffected rests on weak evidence.
The cost-per-ton comparison is conceptually valuable but partially a strawman, since the alternatives are computed without the harmonized benefits the MVPF includes.

sonnet.label: partial
sonnet.reason: Both flag that cap-and-trade results rest on thin evidence, but B11 focuses on strong extrapolations rather than the small number of studies.

papers.title: Does the Squeaky Wheel Get More Grease? The Direct and Indirect Effects of Citizen Participation on Environmental Governance in China

human_issues.text: Claims about general equilibrium effects are overstated: the design captures only local effects bounded by regulator capacity, and does not capture across-prefecture or wider leakage, which is a key concern in environmental policy.
human_issues.quote: the claim that general equilibrium effects are estimated needs caveating as just local general equilibrium effects are mediated

model_issues.text: Figure 3b shows positive and apparently significant pre-period coefficients for T2, contradicting the text's 'no pre-treatment effect' claim; with a 7-week post-COVID pre-period and T2's higher baseline violations (Table 2), mean reversion may inflate DiD estimates.
Heavy-tailed SO2 concentrations (SD ≈ 4× mean) with no reported winsorizing, log transforms or outlier robustness; a few pipes could drive the emissions results.

The ambient SO2 GE result (3.5%, p<0.1) is implausibly large relative to the firm-level effects and the 25 pp saturation difference, appears concentrated in late-year winter weeks, and is over-interpreted as confirming no data manipulation.
GE tests for control firms are underpowered (only 5% control in high-saturation prefectures) and cannot rule out meaningful crowd-out; the treatment-firm GE effect is significant only at 10%.

Mechanism evidence (T2B visibility) rests on 662 appeals with p≈0.05–0.10 and regulator-reported Weibo replies; this measures communicative responsiveness more than enforcement, and the firm-level follow-up is marginal and contaminated by cross-over.

The 'regulators tilt from growth toward avoiding unrest' interpretation is not sharply distinguished from alternatives (superior visibility/accountability, firm reputation, platform processing); the null escalation-threat arms are imprecise, and the term-cycle heterogeneity is observational and ambiguous.
No multiple-hypothesis correction across many arms, outcomes and heterogeneity cuts; no discussion of adherence to the registered pre-analysis plan.

The cost-benefit extrapolation is loose: unexplained derivation of the 9.2%/2.9% reductions, linear scaling to 51,000 appeals ignoring capacity, levies treated as a lower-bound benefit, and verification costs omitted.
Total-emissions conclusions rest on imprecise null effects on CEMS-reported flows.
Reporting inconsistencies: µg vs mg units between text and tables, percentage points written as percent, and a confusingly labeled one-sided test (H0: T1<T2).
Ethical issues (purchased likes via bot accounts, concealed volunteer affiliation, regulators as unconsenting subjects) are under-discussed.
Replication depends on administrative MEE data and a human-judgment violation-verification step; code and data availability are not clearly stated beyond a data appendix link.

codex.label: partial
codex.reason: Both argue that the general-equilibrium evidence cannot rule out important displacement or leakage, with B24 extending the concern beyond prefectures.

sonnet.label: partial
sonnet.reason: Both concern limits of the GE/spillover analysis and inability to rule out leakage or crowd-out.

papers.title: The Returns to Science In the Presence of Technological Risks

human_issues.text: AI risk is excluded from the technical risks being assessed, even though the evaluator's reading of the XPT shows AI risk estimates are far higher than bio risk estimates for both superforecasters and domain experts. Stipulating AI out appears to stack the deck toward accelerating science, and the stipulation's justification is unconvincing.
human_issues.quote: 'stipulating out' AI risk from the technical risks being assessed seems to indeed stack the deck

human_issues.text: Some claims in the paper, such as that the case for science is murkier only under bio risk, or that the title and framing imply a broader conclusion about technological risk, overreach relative to the modelling stipulation.
human_issues.quote: Perhaps the best example[^11] (besides the title of the work) can be found in early in the executive summary:

model_issues.text: The counterfactual (pausing all science for one year) is used to value marginal metascience acceleration; average and marginal value may differ greatly, and this equivalence is assumed, not argued.

Key parameters are judgmental and loosely evidenced: g = 0.75G via an 'arbitrary' 50%/20% split, 56.25% of health gains attributed to science, h = 7 months, T = 74 years (diffusion lag inferred from income/life-expectancy convergence), and p = 0.98.
No joint uncertainty propagation (e.g., Monte Carlo); robustness is one-at-a-time, and stated ranges (d* in 0.1–0.4%) are asserted rather than derived.

Peril calibration imposes a step-function hazard on XPT medians, mixes forecaster populations for regime-exit adjustments, assumes within-bin mortality of 2% and 20%, chooses t1/q1 by judgment, and relies on only 14 biosecurity experts; medians across questions need not cohere.
Headline returns are highly sensitive to population ethics and long-run health dynamics: about 330x in the baseline versus about 69x in the realistic-health model, with no formal reconciliation.
Extinction results reduce to break-even λ tables; the decisive policy question depends on an unknowable E[V*] and on which forecaster group is trusted.
Arguments for preferring superforecasters (intersubjective accuracy, correlated pessimism, one Ackerman tally) are suggestive but weak and asymmetric.
The model scope omits other science-driven risks (AI, nuclear), treats d as constant and persistent, and leaves racing to safety unquantified.
The policy recommendation (treat acceleration and risk separately; ~6% chance science is net harmful) multiplies subjective, assumed-independent probabilities and is not derived from the model.

Many internal inconsistencies: 70x/60x/68x; '0.13-15%'; 20x/140x vs 18x/143x/150x; dx 0.00385% vs 0.02286%; q1 0.53% vs 0.58%; 15 vs 20-year break-even label; 0.16% vs 0.1545%; footnote 12 error; $2.4trn vs $2.3trn; dangling references to 'equation (35)' and 'section xx'.
Replication materials (Python code, spreadsheet) are referenced but not clearly archived; the realistic-health model is hard to reproduce exactly.

codex.label: partial
codex.reason: Both identify the exclusion of AI risk as a central scope limitation, though B1 also includes nuclear risk and other modelling assumptions.

codex.label: partial
codex.reason: Both identify a mismatch between broad technological-risk implications and a model restricted to selected risks, though A11 focuses on overclaimed prose.

sonnet.label: partial
sonnet.reason: Both criticize the model's scope for omitting AI (and other) science-driven risks, though B1 adds nuclear, constancy of d, and racing.

papers.title: Global potential for natural regeneration in deforested tropical regions

human_issues.text: The evaluator has low confidence in the 215 Mha figure as an accurate biophysical potential estimate and notes that the spatial distribution of results is biased toward regions with low anthropogenic disturbance.
human_issues.quote: I have low confidence in the estimated 215 Mha being an accurate figure on biophysical potential.

human_issues.text: Temporal leakage from predictors (e.g., NPP 2000-2015, burned area 2001-2017) that overlap the regeneration outcome period and may be influenced by regeneration itself, creating reverse causality and inflating retrospective accuracy.
human_issues.quote: Predictor variables averaged or derived from periods overlapping or extending beyond the 2000 start date of the regeneration outcome (e.g., NPP 2000-2015, burned area 2001--2017) may incorporate information influenced by the regeneration itself

human_issues.text: Uncertainty is underestimated: the RF model's minimal uncertainty ignores the large uncertainty from the Fagan et al. accuracy assessment (31.6 ± 11.9 Mha), which would widen the interval for the omission-corrected estimate (about 189 Mha).
human_issues.quote: The current approach (reporting just minimal uncertainty from the RF model)  ignores this driving source of uncertainty.

human_issues.text: The paper does not use stratification techniques known to mitigate omission error effects on area estimates for rare classes; the evaluator suggests a buffer-based stratification near forest edges, supported by the finding that most potential regrowth lies within 300 m of forest edges.
human_issues.quote: The paper does not appear to leverage stratification techniques known to mitigate the impact of omission errors on area estimates, particularly for rare classes like forest gain

human_issues.text: The focus on extensive gains in forest area neglects intensive regrowth (canopy recovery within existing forest pixels), so the estimate of natural regrowth potential is incomplete; at minimum the results need reframing with this caveat, as the abstract implies the 215 Mha is all potential regrowth.
human_issues.quote: makes it sound like this is all potential regrowth, not just extensive gain potential, and prioritization based solely on extensive gain ignores significant potential within existing forest areas.

model_issues.text: 1. Random forest scores from a model trained on 50/50 balanced samples are interpreted as calibrated per-pixel probabilities and summed to give 'expected area' (215 Mha); with rare true prevalence this inflates area and makes the headline figure largely an artefact of the sampling design.
2. Reported confidence intervals (e.g., 214.78–215.22 Mha) are implausibly narrow, unexplained, and ignore model, label, covariate and structural uncertainty.

3. Validation relies on random (non-spatially-blocked) points; the paper's own distance-band analysis shows balanced accuracy near 75% at 6–8 km, yet 87.9% is used as the headline. Calibration, AUC and precision at realistic prevalence are not reported.

4. Training labels come from a product with very low area-based producer's accuracy (18.7% in the humid biome); widespread omitted regrowth is labelled as non-regeneration, introducing spatially structured bias that is not quantified.

5. The model is trained on realised regrowth (driven by abandonment, markets, tenure) but socioeconomic covariates are dropped and the output is framed as 'biophysical potential'; persistence and reclearance are not modelled.

6. The dominant predictors (forest density, distance to forest) are partly mechanical for edge-located 30-m regrowth detections, and 2018 tree cover used in prediction includes regrowth itself; the 'potential' largely maps forest-edge and mosaic pixels.

7. Regional carbon estimates (11.1 + 5.42 + 3.1 = 19.6 Gt) do not sum to the global 23.4 Gt, and the comparative framings (90.5% of losses, 26.9% of potential, 0.8 vs ~1 Gt C/yr) are not clearly reconciled.

8. Variable importance is inconsistent: forest density and distance to forest rank lowest by mean decrease in accuracy but highest by Gini, without discussion. Figure inconsistencies include the number of variables (8 vs 10) and Fig. 3d axis errors.
9. The carbon estimate ignores existing biomass, permanence, leakage and additionality, yet the paper suggests the maps can identify offset locations with high additionality and permanence.
10. The 2030 projection assumes 2000–2016 conditions persist and uses 1970–2000 climate; climate change effects are treated only qualitatively.
11. Code is available only on request, and several preprocessing steps (ArcGIS, the WDPA China additions) limit exact reproducibility, although the output rasters are openly released.

codex.label: partial
codex.reason: Both question the 215 Mha map because its distribution reflects low-disturbance realised regeneration rather than pure biophysical potential.

codex.label: related_but_distinct
codex.reason: Both challenge uncertainty around the headline area estimate, but A9 concerns omission-error-aware stratification and B10 concerns implausibly narrow intervals overall.

codex.label: exact
codex.reason: Both say the reported confidence interval is far too narrow because it omits major label and model-related uncertainty.

codex.label: partial
codex.reason: Both identify temporal outcome leakage from forest-related predictors that can inflate retrospective model performance, though they cite different covariates.

sonnet.label: partial
sonnet.reason: Both argue that the reported uncertainty is too narrow because it omits input-label and other sources of uncertainty.

sonnet.label: partial
sonnet.reason: Both identify predictors that overlap with or are influenced by the regrowth outcome itself (2018 tree cover; NPP and burned area over the outcome period).

papers.title: Economic vs. Epidemiological Approaches to Measuring the Human Capital Impacts of Infectious Disease Elimination

human_issues.text: The paper does not sufficiently examine the key assumption behind reduced-form studies: that a worse disease environment in terms of mortality is highly correlated with a worse disease environment for survivors. Evidence on whether this holds for measles is needed.
human_issues.quote: The underlying assumption of most of these reduced-form papers is that a worse disease environment in terms of mortality is likely highly correlated with a worse disease environment for those who survive.

model_issues.text: The epidemiological 'share ever infected' measure has little credible state-by-cohort variation once cohort FEs are included. It is near one for all pre-vaccine cohorts and relies on a national vaccination series, so instability and sign flips likely reflect measurement error rather than irrelevance of infection.

The headline claim that severity matters more than infection rates is not identified. The comparison pits a cross-sectionally rich proxy against a noisy timing-only measure, and severity mechanisms (e.g., age at infection) are never directly tested.

The reduced-form design lacks event-study and pre-trend evidence, state- or region-specific cohort trends, and placebo exposures. These matter because pre-vaccine measles mortality likely correlates with Southern and poverty-related trends and with concurrent 1960s policies (Medicaid, Head Start, desegregation, food stamps).

Reporting rates are estimated from 1950–1960 data and assumed time-invariant. Surveillance likely changed after vaccine introduction, biasing post-1963 infection estimates; implausible pre-vaccine declines (e.g., Arkansas) signal model misspecification.
The mortality 'validation' is partly mechanical. Outcome deaths at ages 0–5 for cohorts 1959–1963 overlap with the 1959–1963 measles mortality used to construct the reduced-form exposure.

The outbreak-prediction tests mainly validate short-run dynamics, partly driven by births and reporting scaling. The comparison with the reduced-form measure is uninformative because a level × post dummy cannot predict annual fluctuations under state and year FEs.

Treatment timing is crude. All cohorts born up to 1963 are coded as fully unexposed to the vaccine, ignoring catch-up vaccination of children born in the late 1950s and early 1960s; birth year imputed from age adds misclassification near the cutoff.
Inference relies on 41 clusters without small-cluster corrections, and many outcomes are tested without multiple-hypothesis adjustment.
Several robustness claims (alternative reporting rates, age-dependent risk) are asserted rather than shown, and Figure A5 covers only two outcomes.
The inference from similarity to Atwood (2022) that reported incidence proxies severity is speculative. Policy extrapolation to low-income countries goes beyond the evidence.
There is no replication code; table units, decile/lag labelling and some figure labels are unclear, and typos and inconsistencies in state exclusions remain.

sonnet.label: partial
sonnet.reason: Both question the untested assumption that mortality (or reported incidence) proxies the disease environment or severity for survivors.

papers.title: Meaningfully reducing consumption of meat and animal products is an unsolved problem: A meta-analysis

human_issues.text: Data extraction was performed by a single author without any check of the tool's appropriateness or consistency of application, and no results of such checks are reported.
human_issues.quote: The first author extracted all data.

human_issues.text: The outcome selection hierarchy creates a paradox in which an outcome is treated as sufficient evidence in one study but ignored in another when both are available.
human_issues.quote: This creates a paradox where outcome B is treated as sufficient evidence in one context but ignored in another, even when available.

model_issues.text: 1. Single-author data extraction and effect-size conversion, with inclusion decisions also primarily by one author, and no reported double coding or reliability check; there is no preregistered protocol.
2. Three inclusion/exclusion decisions were made after data collection began (RPM category, substitution studies, no-choice interventions), creating scope for researcher degrees of freedom.
3. 'Unspecified null' outcomes are imputed as SMD = 0.01 without a reported sensitivity analysis; this may bias pooled estimates toward zero.

4. Internal inconsistencies: the abstract has a duplicated, contradictory sentence; psychology counts differ between the text (9 studies/12 estimates) and Table 1 (19/32); region counts sum to 40, not 41.
5. The marginal-study comparison (0.07 vs 0.20) is confounded by many study differences and cannot isolate methodological rigor as the cause of larger effects.
6. The RPM vs MAP gap is attributed speculatively to substitution, though RPM studies differ systematically in population (clinical/health trials) and intervention intensity.
7. Effects are not translated into practical units (grams, servings, % reduction) or cost-effectiveness, so the normative 'unsolved problem' claim lacks a decision-relevant benchmark.
8. Using the longest follow-up per intervention conflates effect decay with intervention efficacy; there is no analysis of effects by follow-up length despite the paper's emphasis on durability.
9. Risk-of-bias variables (self-report vs objective outcomes, preregistration) were collected but not analyzed as moderators in the main text; self-reported outcomes risk social desirability bias.

10. Choice architecture conclusions rest on 3 estimates (including a fish-sauce study of questionable relevance, also double-classified); exclusion criteria remove the default/no-choice interventions most relevant to institutional policy.
11. Subgroup and moderator estimates with 2–3 studies have uninformative CIs under RVE; the claimed decline over time is not statistically supported.
12. The search is non-systematic and the PRISMA diagram has oddities (no duplicates removed, no screening exclusions), which limits reproducibility of the search.

codex.label: exact
codex.reason: Both identify single-author data extraction without an adequate check of consistent or appropriate application.

codex.label: partial
codex.reason: Both identify bias or inconsistency introduced by a hierarchy that selects one outcome or time point while discarding alternatives.

sonnet.label: exact
sonnet.reason: Both flag single-author data extraction without reliability or consistency checks.

papers.title: Accelerating Vaccine Innovation for Emerging Infectious Diseases via Parallel Discovery

human_issues.text: The paper is not convincing as a model of the future of vaccine development in its current form.
human_issues.quote: In its current form I do not find it convincing as a model of the future of vaccine development

human_issues.text: The paper's conclusions do not reflect that sensitivity analyses alter the results, and the abstract omits this. The evaluator also flags that the discussion of low- and middle-income countries affordability conflicts with the premise of private profit.
human_issues.quote: yet in the abstract you don't mention this sensitivity analysis, or indeed any of your sensitivity analyses, alter your conclusions

human_issues.text: The 10% annual discount rate is very high relative to the 3-5% typically used in health economic evaluations.
human_issues.quote: an annual discount rate of 10% is very high. Typically 3-5% is used in health economic evaluations

model_issues.text: 1. Every candidate that clears phase 2 is advanced to a $150M phase 3 trial during outbreaks despite full revenue cannibalization. This mechanically generates the negative NPV, the 'higher PoS lowers NPV' result and the portfolio-size result, which are presented as substantive findings rather than artifacts.

2. Demand is fixed at 10M doses per local outbreak regardless of epidemic size (e.g., 75 Marburg cases versus 500k Chikungunya cases), Lassa has a 100% annual outbreak probability, and disease X gets 1B doses. The infection counts in Table 1 apparently do not drive revenue.

3. Phase 3 efficacy trials (30,000 subjects, 14 months, 80.9% PoS) are assumed feasible during small outbreaks of rare pathogens, which is unrealistic. The accelerated phase 1/2 pathway parameters are unsupported.

4. 'Epidemics prevented' is ill-defined given that trials start only after an outbreak begins. The claim that social benefits far exceed the financial losses is asserted without any QALY or cost-benefit computation.

5. The correlation metric (ρ = 1 − d from four biological similarity scores) is ad hoc and its inputs are unreported. The latent-Gaussian thresholding does not yield the stated binary correlations, and cross-phase dependence is unspecified.

6. Sensitivity analysis is one-at-a-time and omits key drivers: discount rate, horizon or terminal value, phase-3 cost, doses per outbreak, outbreak probabilities and disease X parameters. There is no probabilistic or global sensitivity analysis.
7. The annualized return metric is undefined. The large discrepancy with the predecessor study (−61% versus −6%) is not reconciled.

8. Pricing assumes US list prices, with no modeling of buyers (governments or LMICs), procurement mechanisms, advance commitments or price-elastic demand, which limits the policy interpretation of the $69–78 breakeven prices.
9. The securitization/debt structure motivating the 'megafund' is not modeled. Results describe an unlevered portfolio, so implications for bond-market investors are untested.
10. Human challenge trial modeling only swaps phase-3 cost and duration, so the conclusion that HCTs are insufficient is assumption-driven.

11. There are minor inconsistencies: $9.5B versus $10B public funding; 'financial benefits of diversification' language despite diversification adding cost; and some unexplained distributional summaries.
12. No code or full parameter set is released and the distance-metric inputs are missing, which impedes replication. Industry co-authorship is disclosed.

codex.label: exact
codex.reason: Both identify the discount rate as an important unexamined or inadequately justified driver of results.

sonnet.label: related_but_distinct
sonnet.reason: B2 notes LMIC affordability conflicts with private profit premise, loosely relating to A2's missing LMIC buyers.

sonnet.label: partial
sonnet.reason: A6 lists discount rate among omitted sensitivity drivers; B9 criticizes the 10% discount rate.

sonnet.label: related_but_distinct
sonnet.reason: B10 is a generic criticism of model credibility.

papers.title: When do Nudges Increase Welfare?

human_issues.text: The experimental incentives may be too weak and the complexity of the design may inhibit rational responses; the authors did not discuss the cognitive load imposed by their design or the known issues with multiple price lists.
human_issues.quote: Sadly, the authors did not present any discussion as to this inherent cognitive load imposed by their design.

model_issues.text: 1. Cars sample trims 39% of completers, including on the outcome (WTP change) and on estimated bias. Untrimmed estimates (Table A5) differ dramatically in covariances, variance and ATE, and welfare is not recomputed under these alternatives.
2. Welfare estimates (ΔW) are reported without standard errors. Cars ΔW(t=0)≈−0.07 depends on Cov[γ,τ] whose SE is roughly three times its point estimate, so the sign is essentially undetermined.

3. Label-specific cars results flip sign (Full MPG negative; Average cost, Personalized cost and SmartWay positive, including at the optimal tax). This undermines the pooled 'labels reduce welfare' message for cars.
4. Var[τ] identification attributes any label-induced increase in response dispersion (confusion, transient noise) to welfare-relevant heterogeneity. Persistence of individual τ is untested.

5. Normality assumptions are clearly violated: there is a large mass at zero WTP change, interval censoring from the adaptive MPL, and median imputation for off-list responses. Only a limited non-normal check (drinks covariance) is provided.

6. Bias measurement is weak. Cars bias relies on hypothetical gas-free WTP and implies implausibly high (44%) inattention. Drinks bias uses imported proxy mappings (κ) and a homogeneous externality, and Assumption 1 (measurement error independent of τ) is strong.
7. Population moments are used in place of the marginal-consumer moments the theory requires; the marginal-sample estimates (Table A6) differ materially.

8. Measured psychic costs, which are large relative to the computed surplus effects, are set to zero in the quantitative analysis. This makes the drinks welfare ranking depend on an omitted dominant term.

9. Pass-through and markup inputs are rough literature averages with μ=0, and the t=0 welfare sign is sensitive to plausible ρ ranges. The demand slope comes from the experimental rather than the market demand curve.

10. External validity is limited: hypothetical car leases, a Facebook sample of heavy soda drinkers, on-screen labels in a simplified binary choice, possible experimenter demand, and within-subject consistency pressure.
11. The discrete label is analyzed with a local, marginal-σ formula under an assumption of linearity in σ, an approximation that is not validated.

sonnet.label: related_but_distinct
sonnet.reason: Both link design complexity/confusion to noisy responses.

papers.title: The animal welfare cost of meat: evidence from a survey of hypothetical scenarios among Belgian consumers

human_issues.text: The claim that the findings show a social consensus that reducing intensive farming is beneficial over-reads the results given the reported heterogeneity, comprehension issues, and unreliable point estimates.
human_issues.quote: the results indicate that there could be a social consensus on the fact that reducing intensive farming would be beneficial

model_issues.text: 1. Construct validity: the pill thought experiment elicits human imaginative attitudes and income-scaled money metrics, not animal welfare. The separability and δa=1 claims are asserted, not tested, and duration misunderstanding and identity-aversion are likely.

2. The headline 'median 10 €/kg' for chicken rests on N=57 high-confidence WTA respondents. In the full consistent sample the median relative WTA is 0, and all median WTP values are 0, so the abstract overstates robustness.
3. Mean estimates (≈50,000 €/kg chicken) are dominated by extreme responses and swing several-fold (up to more than €1m per pig) with ad hoc outlier and winsorisation choices.

4. No standard errors or confidence intervals are reported for any WTP/WTA estimate, and there is no pre-registration. Exclusion rules (median-confidence cut, '1,000,000 happens to be useful' truncation, inconsistency criteria) are discretionary and inconsistently applied (exclusion for medians, weighting for means).

5. The chicken-vs-beef 'two orders of magnitude' result is mechanically driven by dividing similar per-animal valuations by meat yield. This assumes equal per-life costs and ignores lifespan, breeding animals and dairy, and the measure is itself scope-insensitive (pig ≈ chicken).

6. Heavy attrition and filtering (500 → 301 → 240 → ~57–66 for medians) with a WTP/WTA split leaves very small, possibly selected samples. Subgroup tests are underpowered, and order effects cannot be assessed.

7. Internal inconsistencies: 'three measures' vs two in Table 4; the claim that chicken MWTP is lowest contradicts the guessed-WTP means (chicken 8.7 > pork 7.1); and Table 7 cites Table 4 instead of Table 3.

8. The Table 7 carbon-tax calculation mixes a Belgian survey with US data, keeps counting internalised climate costs as external, has hard-to-reproduce consumption changes, and reports the +$150,000/yr mean-based figure without derivation.

9. Policy recommendations (flat meat tax, prioritising chicken reduction) are not derived from an optimal-tax analysis. The backfire result relies on the mean WTA that the author deems unreliable, while the median shows net external costs fall.

10. Ad hoc interpretive steps: using hypothetical-bias multipliers to equate the median absolute WTA with 'real mean WTP', a loss-function discussion that ends inconclusive, and loose literature 'correspondences'.
11. The WTA–WTP gap is huge, and choosing WTA on rights-based grounds is a normative choice that drives magnitudes by orders of magnitude.
12. No data, code or full survey instrument are shared, limiting reproducibility. There are minor typos and reference errors (e.g., the 'is welfare optimizing' wording, citation details).

codex.label: partial
codex.reason: Both argue that the paper overstates what its fragile and heterogeneous results establish, though the claimed conclusion differs.

papers.title: Pharmaceutical Pricing and R&D as a Global Public Good

human_issues.text: The primary regression is overly simplistic and may suffer from omitted variable bias; other factors correlated with GDP are not included, so the estimated effect of GDP may be overstated or misattributed and results should be interpreted with caution.
human_issues.quote: The primary regression analyzed in the paper is overly simplistic and may be subject to omitted variable bias.

human_issues.text: Healthcare system structure (private versus public financing) is omitted from the model and could significantly affect pharmaceutical R&D contributions, so it should be included as an indicator or index.
human_issues.quote: The distinction between private and public healthcare systems could significantly impact pharmaceutical R&D contributions.

human_issues.text: The framework focuses only on the demand side and ignores supply-side factors such as production costs, regulatory barriers, and firm strategies that shape pricing and R&D incentives.
human_issues.quote: The current framework focuses on the demand side, with country contributions driving innovation.

human_issues.text: The paper's contribution relative to prior work on drug prices through a similar lens is not clearly articulated.
human_issues.quote: they could more clearly articulate their unique contribution in relation to previous work.

model_issues.text: 1. Regressing log contribution (∝ branded sales) on log GDP is largely mechanical: high R² and positive elasticity follow from spending scaling with economic size, not from Nash/alliance behavior.

2. An elasticity above 1 does not test Olson's exploitation hypothesis. It is equally consistent with income-elastic health demand, Nash bargaining, or value-based pricing, and population versus income per capita are not separated in reported results.

3. Contributions are highly sensitive to the assumed common MC. Using Turkey's price sets its contribution to zero by construction, and the 24% CEA adjustment and cross-country uniform MC are rough. Negative or zero values are dropped from log models (selection).

4. Treating current price–MC margins on existing drugs as R&D 'contributions' conflates past sunk-cost recovery, marketing and rents with expected future returns. US prices are not a sovereign contribution choice, so the Nash model maps poorly onto the data.
5. Single-observation country dummies with heteroskedasticity-robust SEs (leverage = 1) give unreliable inference. Text claims of 5% significance for the dummies contradict Tables 4–5.

6. Sensitivity analyses (linear form, adding dropped countries, out-of-pocket share, CE thresholds, per-capita/population split) are described but not reported, and control-variable sources are undocumented.
7. Rejecting 'pure free riding' attacks a strawman. The 27–33% ROW share is descriptive and close to prior estimates, adding limited new evidence.

8. The normative claim that the US underpays (cost per QALY vs. VSL-based WTP) compares average with marginal quantities and does not identify the Lindahl condition. Policy recommendations are not derived from the empirical results.
9. Footnote 12's arc-elasticity computation is incorrect: doubling GDP implies ≈135% increase, not 145%.
10. Numerous internal inconsistencies (ROW totals $106.8B / $110.4B / $115B, US shares 66/67% and 73/72%, UK sales $23B / $23.7B) plus citation and date mismatches and misspellings.
11. Small single-year cross-section (n≈30), no causal identification, and no code or compiled data released, though the inputs are public.

papers.title: Does online fundraising increase charitable giving? A nationwide field experiment on Facebook

human_issues.text: The authors deviated from the pre-analysis plan in several ways (covariates, trimming, diff-in-diff, outcome choices) without clearly flagging these deviations, raising type-I error concerns.
human_issues.quote: I think they should be more careful to specify where they have stuck to the plan, and where they have deviated from it.

model_issues.text: 1. Headline revenue effect is significant only at p<0.1 (long-term) and not significant in the short term; it depends on lagged-DV adjustment given a non-significant pretreatment imbalance.

2. Profitability claims ('campaign was profitable') are overstated: the immediate return CI is 0.15–2.74, and the long-run €2.53 rests on an ad hoc LTV multiplier of 1.75 also applied to repeat donors.

3. Crowding-out evidence is weak and specification-dependent: there are significant pretreatment imbalances in the alliance data, only DiD estimates reach p<0.1, and only 1 of 4 betterplace coefficients is significant. Yet strong conclusions about money being 'lost to the charitable sector' are drawn.

4. Spillover estimates imply a total effect about 10x the direct effect (≈€170 vs €17.7 per million per day), which is implausible and unreconciled with the profitability analysis. The neighbour-share measure may proxy for geography or urban density.

5. No multiple-testing correction across outcomes, horizons, arms, data sources, decompositions, and 12 heterogeneity splits. Heterogeneity results are presented as targeting advice without caveats about exploratory status.

6. Deviations from preregistration (blocking variable, added allocation arm) are noted, but the paper does not distinguish preregistered from exploratory analyses (competition, spillovers, heterogeneity).
7. The claim that click metrics mislead rests on comparing significant click differences with non-significant donation differences. The click proportions tests treat impressions as independent.
8. Standard errors are robust but not spatially clustered, despite evidence of geographic spillovers; this may understate uncertainty (randomization inference partly mitigates this).
9. External validity is overstated ('no matter the specific campaign design, online fundraising works'): there is one charity, one country, one season, two videos, and a 2017 platform environment.

10. Low treatment intensity (~10% of reachable users received an impression) and endogenous spend allocation in the free-allocation arm complicate interpretation of the arm comparisons and per-impression returns.
11. Replication barriers: there is no mention of a code/data package and the donation data are proprietary partner aggregates; several robustness claims are 'not presented here'.
12. Presentation issues: Figure 1 uses truncated axes, Table 7 is mislabeled ('Long-term' includes short-term), and the heterogeneity table is hard to read.

codex.reason: Both say the paper fails to distinguish preregistered analyses from exploratory deviations, creating excess analytic freedom.

sonnet.label: exact
sonnet.reason: Both say deviations from the pre-analysis plan are not clearly flagged or separated from exploratory analyses.

papers.title: How Much Would Reducing Lead Exposure Improve Childrens Learning in the Developing World?

human_issues.text: The evaluator asks for the minimum and maximum number of effect estimates contributed by a single study, given 286 estimates from 47 studies.
human_issues.quote:
It would be useful to know the minimum and maximum
number of estimates contributed by a single study.

model_issues.text: The benchmark -0.115 SD (Table 2 col. 4) has SE 0.100 and is statistically insignificant (95% CI ≈ -0.31 to +0.08), yet it is presented as a firm benchmark in the abstract and policy simulations.

The benchmark constant extrapolates to a reference category no result satisfies (LMIC reading/maths with full controls), supported by only three LMIC achievement studies; the shift from -0.154 to -0.115 rests on six individually insignificant covariates.

The Linakis re-expression algorithm, applied to roughly 76% of estimates, substantially understates log effects at low BLL in the authors' own validation (Table A3); this likely biases pooled estimates toward zero and is not discussed.

Publication-bias correction is model-dependent: the PEESE term barely moves the estimate, while Egger/PET gives -0.085; most of the reduction comes from the parental-education control, conflating confounding with selection.

The conclusion that the true causal effect is 'much smaller' conflicts with the IV evidence, which uniformly shows larger effects (consistent with measurement-error attenuation); the IV table mixes non-comparable outcomes and exposure measures.
The Oster bounding uses only 6 estimates from 5 studies with default δ=1 and Rmax=1.3, too thin to generalise a one-third confounding share.
Systematic-review methods are weak: Google Scholar title-only search, single-reviewer screening, no protocol or pre-registration, and no risk-of-bias assessment.
Very high heterogeneity (I² of 77–97%) and pooling of prenatal and childhood, concurrent and lagged exposure leave the average effect hard to interpret.
The policy simulation formula 'β×(μ−0.5)' appears to mix log and level units, and log-linear extrapolation to 0.5 µg/dL (or 0.01 in Table 4) generates implausibly large gains.
Intervention BLL reductions come mostly from before-after studies; the simulations ignore exposure timing (early-life versus school-age), persistence, and costs despite cost-effectiveness claims.
Mapping within-sample SD effects onto World Bank HLO points (SD=100) assumes comparable SD units across very different test distributions.
Internal inconsistencies: a CI described as the range of estimates, sign errors, -0.13 versus -0.115, an unsupported 'over half the gap' claim in the conclusion, and mismatched Oster figure notes.
No data or code are provided despite many judgment-laden imputations and conversions, hindering replication.

papers.title: Urban Forests: Environmental Health Values and Risks

human_issues.text: The contrast in Figure 5 between PM2.5 persisting over multiple days and pollen not doing so is not explained; the evaluator asks whether this is consistent with the science literature.
human_issues.quote: Based on Figure 5, PM~2.5~ "sticks around" for longer

model_issues.text: 1. The daily 'upwind NDVI' variation comes entirely from wind direction, since NDVI is monthly. Wind direction directly drives Beijing PM2.5 (clean northerlies from vegetated mountains, polluted southerlies), and no wind-direction fixed effects or meteorological controls are included, so the vegetation effect is confounded.
2. The downwind placebo and event study do not address this confound: downwind NDVI is also a function of wind direction, and the leads and lags largely reflect wind-direction persistence.

3. PM2.5 elasticities of about -0.4 to -0.5 and pollen elasticities of about 0.7 to 1 per log upwind NDVI are physically implausible as filtration and emission effects, and far exceed deposition-based estimates.

4. Applying cross-sectional, cross-direction elasticities to a decade-long temporal NDVI increase, measured at planting sites rather than across the upwind cone, likely overstates the 4.2% PM2.5 and 7.4% pollen attribution.

5. Robustness is overstated: the PM2.5 effect is null at 5 km, only marginal at the 10 km all-grid baseline and insignificant with year×month fixed effects, and robust only at 15 km. Some downwind coefficients are positive and significant.

6. The Section 4 AOD gradient may be mechanical, because MAIAC retrievals depend on surface reflectance. It also uses a 1-km product in 200 m distance bins and measures column rather than ground-level pollution.

7. The pollen–ER regressions are OLS without baseline weather controls, use few clusters (16 districts), and proxy residence by hospital district. Medication-based 'sensory' classification appears dominated by antibiotic eye drops, so allergic causes are not clearly identified.

8. The cost-benefit chain mixes literature estimates (short-run Olympic mortality, long-run cardiovascular mortality, a 4× lag scaling, a low VSL), has no uncertainty propagation, and claims payback within a decade while its own numbers imply about 12–15 years.

9. There are multiple internal inconsistencies: 20 vs 12 pollen stations, wind data years, identical observation counts for the pollen and health panels, differing elasticities across sections, a wrong CNY–USD conversion, 0.25% vs 0.1–0.4% of health spending, and 'two-fold' vs 'three times' spending ratios.

10. The pollen cost estimate ('one-ninth') rests on a loose argument about inpatient spending shares rather than direct estimation, and omits non-ER costs such as medication, productivity and cognition.
11. There is no replication package or data statement. The claims data are proprietary, and sharing of the digitized MMP polygons is not mentioned.

papers.title: Selecting the Most Effective Nudge: Evidence from a Large-Scale Experiment on Immunization

human_issues.text: The evaluator's main criticism is that the paper's cost-effectiveness argument, that immunization remains the best use of money even when many payments go to inframarginal households, should be emphasized more and placed earlier, perhaps in the introduction, because it shapes the paper's bottom-line policy takeaway.
human_issues.quote: should probably be emphasized more and earlier on (perhaps in the introduction)

model_issues.text: 1. Standard errors are clustered at the sub-center level, but incentives were randomized across 140 PHCs. Inference for all incentive-containing pooled policies (including the headline 44% policy) is likely understated, and footnote 34 is inconsistent with the design.

2. The LASSO penalty (p-threshold 5×10⁻¹³) was chosen ex post via an 'admissibility' procedure that inspects results. The best immunization policy switches below λ ≈ 0.47, the admissible window is narrow, and the bootstrap selects the headline best policy in only 77% of samples.

3. Theoretical guarantees assume iid homoskedastic Gaussian errors, exact sparsity/beta-min, and K = o(√n). None of these clearly hold empirically (K = 75 vs ~915 villages, weighted clustered panel data).

4. The winner's-curse adjustment combined with model selection and asymptotic normality is acknowledged as unproven. Hybrid confidence intervals condition on the selected support and λ and ignore selection uncertainty; inference is only pointwise.
5. Numerical inconsistencies: CI [0.032, 6.25] in the text vs [0.32, 6.25] in Table 1; [0.003, 0.004] vs [0.003, 0.005]; unexplained observation counts (204, 814); multiple differing control means.
6. Cost-effectiveness accounting (which costs enter, the control denominator, fixed vs variable costs) is not documented, even though the 'most cost-effective' result is a key policy claim.

7. Dosage orderings (trusted information hub as a higher dose of information hub; SMS saturation as dosage) are researcher-imposed and drive admissible pooling. Trusted information hubs being separately pooled with a negative effect strains this assumption, and sensitivity to alternative orderings is not shown.

8. Simulations are small (5 configurations × 20 draws), use homoskedastic Gaussian errors with large separated effects, and rely partly on TVA-tailored metrics. They do not mimic clustering or weighting.

9. The conclusion overstates: it claims a no-interaction analysis would find 'nothing effective', contradicting the paper's own main-effects results. The complementarity/catalyst mechanism rests on fragile pooled estimates.
10. Proofs contain typos and loose steps (λ vs λ², wrong assumption references, unclear C_min bound, crude sup-norm bound) that should be corrected.
11. The outcome is camp-recorded measles shots per village-month rather than coverage. The substitution check is underpowered, and TVA was not part of the pre-registered analysis.
12. No code or data availability is stated, which limits reproducibility of a complex multi-step pipeline.

codex.reason: Both address the central cost-effectiveness policy conclusion, but A9 challenges undocumented accounting whereas B2 asks for the conclusion to be emphasized earlier.

sonnet.reason: Both concern the cost-effectiveness claim, but A9 says the accounting is undocumented while B2 says the argument should be emphasized earlier.

papers.title: Universal Basic Income: Short-Term Results from a Long-Term Experiment in Kenya

human_issues.text: Effects on other NGOs and their interaction with the cash program may be location-specific and not generalisable; the paper does not describe these NGO activities sufficiently.
human_issues.quote: It would seem very useful to understand more about the activities of these other NGOs

model_issues.text: Cross-arm comparisons (ST vs LS vs LT) are acknowledged to be underpowered, yet the abstract and conclusion emphasize them; many rely on one-sided tests not clearly pre-specified and on p-values of 0.05–0.15.
No multiple-hypothesis correction across the many outcomes and seven tests per column; the mapping to the 10 pre-registered outcome families and any PAP deviations are not documented.

Key mechanism evidence (ROSCAs, land, alcohol) comes from a 2022 phone survey designed after seeing the data, when LT was still receiving transfers and ST had stopped, so the endline LT–ST mechanism is confounded.
Table E.1 shows significant positive price effects for LS (≈+0.33 log CPI) and for LT on agricultural prices, contradicting the text's 'no price change' framing; real effects may be overstated.
Inference relies on Conley spatial errors with unspecified kernel and cutoff and no explicit village clustering; cross-village spillover tests are mentioned but not reported.

Village aggregates combine census data with sample-scaled household survey data, set missing enterprise data to zero, and face 3–4pp differential enterprise-survey response; net revenues ignore own labor.
Attritor composition differs on baseline height-for-age and depression, the very outcomes used for cross-arm interpretation; no Lee bounds or reweighting are provided.
Self-assessed land appreciation (larger than the transfers) is unverifiable, and its interpretation as increased desirability or store-of-value demand is speculative.

The theoretical model is loosely executed: text and figure parameters differ, simulated paths explode to ~1e8, the comparative statics contain errors, and the claim that constraints 'must' play a role in any explanation is too strong.
Numerous text–table inconsistencies (e.g., non-ag enterprise increase stated as 25% vs ~35% in Table 3; 15% vs 11–12% transfer share; wrong table references; 'reduction in labor supply' wording).
Wage evidence relies on elder reports available for only ~60% of villages; reservation-wage evidence is weaker.
No replication package, code, or data availability statement; variable construction is documented only briefly.

papers.title: The Macroeconomic Impact of Climate Change: Global vs. Local Temperature

human_issues.text: The paper does not clearly characterise how far out of sample a 1C temperature change is, since the largest shock in the sample is only 0.3C, so the damage calibration relies on extrapolation the evaluator thinks should be made explicit.
human_issues.quote: A taste request is to characterize - up front - just how out-of-sample a 1C change truly is. The largest [change] in the sample is 0.3C.

human_issues.text: Calibrating response damages to the largest observed shock in the sample, rather than to a 1C change, is suggested as a way to add credibility to the headline estimates.
human_issues.quote: Calibrating response damages to this largest, but not particularly uncommon, shock might add to the credibility of the paper rather than take away from its message.

model_issues.text: 1. Identification rests on ~60 annual observations of one aggregate global temperature shock series (SD ≈0.12°C); the 1°C effect is a linear extrapolation with wide confidence bands and limited power at 6–10 year horizons.

2. Time fixed effects cannot be used, so causal interpretation depends on a short list of global controls; recession dummies and oil prices may be bad controls if temperature affects them, and unobserved global confounders cannot be ruled out.
3. The panel 'corroboration' uses the same aggregate time-series variation and adds no independent identification; Driscoll–Kraay inference with T≈60 may understate uncertainty.

4. The implied magnitudes are not confronted: ENSO-scale shocks would explain a large share of world business-cycle variance, and historical warming supposedly cut world GDP by 19%; no external plausibility checks are offered.

5. The 'shock' raises global temperature by about 0.5°C even after 10 years, which raises questions about whether the filtered series captures transient natural variability or trend-correlated components; the ocean/ENSO-driven variation may not scale like anthropogenic mean warming.

6. Extrapolation from transitory natural variability to permanent, anticipated multi-degree warming relies on linearity, a no-Lucas-critique deconvolution and an argument about limited adaptation, none of which is tested out of sample.

7. The structural damage function (three parameters fitted to 10 noisy IRF points) determines long-run cumulative damages largely through functional form; the fit undershoots the empirical peak, and damages are linear in temperature.

8. SCC assumptions are idiosyncratic: no-growth economy with ρ=2% and γ=1, a 0.75 scaling of the CO2–temperature response, and delta-method CIs that ignore model and climate uncertainty; the US DCC figures are asserted without derivation.

9. The extreme-events mechanism is correlational; the 'two-thirds explained' aggregation chains separately estimated panel coefficients without propagating uncertainty, and distance-weighted external shocks (~5% effects) blur the global/local dichotomy.
10. The rhetoric ('demonstrate', 'six times larger than previously thought') overstates the novelty and certainty relative to growth-effect panel studies and recent extremes-based estimates.
11. Internal inconsistencies: SCC reported as both $1,367 and $1,347; the gap is described as six times, seven times and an order of magnitude; the benchmark shifts between $185 and $178.
12. No replication package is mentioned, and many researcher choices (extreme-event thresholds, smoothing, deconvolution) hinder exact reproduction.

papers.title: Advance Market Commitments: Insights from Theory and Experience

human_issues.text: The evaluator questions whether KLS's results are robust to the choice of comparator class, since rotavirus is the only comparator used; alternative vaccine comparators could yield different counterfactual coverage estimates.
human_issues.quote: there is a reasonable worry over whether the results are robust to a different comparator class of vaccines when estimating the counterfactual impact

model_issues.text: 1. No credible counterfactual for the AMC's effect: the headline '700,000 lives saved' is attributable to PCV rollout, yet the abstract and conclusion framing invite readers to credit the AMC, despite the authors' own acknowledgment that additionality is unknown.
2. The 700,000-lives estimate is not sourced or derived in the main text, and it coincides numerically with the WHO estimate of annual pneumococcal deaths, creating potential confusion.

3. The PCV-versus-rotavirus comparison (convergence about five years faster; fewer shortages) is a single descriptive contrast confounded by differences in prequalification timing, manufacturers, technology, demand, and capacity constraints; no robustness or alternative comparators are offered.
4. Cost-effectiveness ($83/DALY) relies on a 2011 ex ante model at initial prices rather than an ex post evaluation of realized coverage, prices, and epidemiology.

5. The key pricing calibration ($3.50 dominates $2 if refusal risk rises by only 4%) is relegated to an appendix, depends on assumptions about alternative uses of savings, and lacks transparent parameters or sensitivity analysis in the main text.

6. The authors concede that at least one firm would likely have participated at a lower price (continued supply at $2.90), but do not quantify the resulting windfall or reconcile it with their defense of the price level.

7. The authors helped design the pilot; the paper discloses this but does not engage substantively with external critiques (additionality, rents to incumbents, choice of a technologically close target), and it characterizes price critics somewhat dismissively.

8. Theoretical claims (robust underinvestment in capacity; tying funds to capacity commitments) are summarized from a separate working paper without stating assumptions, and their mapping onto how the pilot actually functioned is not evaluated.
9. Price and coverage comparisons with non-GAVI countries and other vaccines do not separate the AMC's effect from GAVI pooled procurement and tiered pricing generally.
10. The discussion of supplier number, Serum Institute entry, and the political economy of target choice is plausible but speculative; Serum Institute entry is confounded by substantial push funding.
11. Limited replicability: no code or data files are referenced in the main text, and key figures and calibrations reside only in the online appendix.

codex.label: partial
codex.reason: Both fault reliance on an inadequate comparator set for estimating the AMC effect, although A4 specifically highlights the pooled-procurement confound.

papers.title: Legalizing Entrepreneurship

human_issues.text: In the panel specification, the non-PEP group shows a noticeable increase in entrepreneurship, which the evaluator finds unexplained; it is unclear whether something changed that could threaten the comparison.
human_issues.quote: It is not that clear to me why those who did not receive it see an increase (albeit much lower) in entrepreneurship (see figure 7). Did something change?

human_issues.text: Results differ between the panel regression and the IV cross-section for the sub-samples in Tables 8 and 9, and the paper does not explain these differences.
human_issues.quote: Here, the results in the panel regression differs from the results using the IV cross-section. It would be important to explain these differences.

model_issues.text: Instrument construction may not isolate rain-driven variation: ActualDelay appears to use realized census numbers (containing non-rain endogenous components) while ExpectedDelay comes from re-ranked model predictions, so ActualDelay minus ExpectedDelay may include non-rain variation.

Over-parameterized prediction model (rain interacted with city FEs, date FEs, squared and binary terms) yields potential-census-number dispersion (Fig. 5) far larger than the ~450-position-per-SD main rain effect implies; robustness to simpler maps and a decomposition of identifying variation are needed.

Inference is likely understated: clustering is reported by family (or by date in Table 5's note, inconsistently), whereas the shock varies at municipality-day level; no randomization inference using the permutations is provided.
Main 2SLS estimates are fragile (Simple model significant only at 10%; point estimates 0.012–0.018 with SEs varying twofold), and the year-by-year confidence intervals include zero until 2022.

Balance table contradicts the text: 'has family in Venezuela' has a normalized difference of 0.35, and no p-values are shown; the complier profile includes an impossible negative share (−0.02) and uses an ad hoc binary instrument.
Effect-size framing overreaches: a LATE is divided by the full-sample mean ('factor of 12') and compared with population native rates ('parity'), mixing estimands.

Formalization and measurement are not ruled out: PEP provides recognized ID that may enable registration of existing activity, and ID-based matching (legal representative only for sociedades) could create treatment-correlated measurement error.

The panel 'relocation vs visa' decomposition is not causally identified (endogenous PEP take-up, common timing); the difference shrinks to marginal significance with individual FEs and trends, yet 'twice as large' is headlined.

The theoretical framework is loosely formalized: no proofs, inconsistent notation (P^D vs P^Z), a binary theory applied to a multi-valued delay instrument, and an undemonstrated convex-weighting claim.

Numerous internal inconsistencies: dates of decree and application windows, take-up rates (60/64/68%), sample sizes, firm counts (442/458/~557), municipality counts, rain-measure definitions, and the first-stage sign described as 'positive'.
Mechanism claims ('investment choices', not subsistence) rest on imprecise heterogeneity splits without direct tests.
No code or data availability; the permutation and prediction pipeline is under-documented, limiting replication.

papers.title: Money (Not) to Burn: Payments for Ecosystem Services to Reduce Crop Residue Burning

human_issues.text: The description of methods does not clarify how the overall amount of the PES payment was set, although the payment level plausibly affects both contract uptake and compliance.
human_issues.quote: The description of the methods should clarify how the overall amount of the PES payment was set, given that this certainly has an impact on the uptake of the contract as well as compliance with it.

model_issues.text: Remote-sensing classifier uses no-burn labels drawn only from treatment-group monitoring (burn labels from both arms), creating risk of treatment-dependent misclassification; the conditional-distribution check in Fig. A.3 is a weak test.

Treatment effects on satellite-measured burning are sensitive to the classification threshold. The upfront-vs-standard difference is p=0.071 under max accuracy, and the upfront effect shrinks to ~0.03 just above the chosen thresholds (Fig. A.5); holdout no-burn accuracy is only 63–76%.
The contract-compliance outcome is undefined for control and requires farmers to call for monitoring, so upfront payment may partly raise engagement or calling rather than not-burning.
Calling standard PES payments 'inframarginal' over-interprets an imprecise null (0.008, SE 0.042); effects as large as the upfront effect cannot be ruled out.

Mechanism evidence on trust relies on a post-treatment, self-reported endline question for a subset of contract signers and is likely contaminated by receipt of the upfront payment; pre-specified heterogeneity by trust and liquidity is null, so the mechanism remains largely unidentified.

Cost-benefit and cost-per-life figures rest on average (not marginal) damages, a $1M VSL, linear dose-response and a 50% burn share applied across states with very different burning rates; headline numbers use the most favourable threshold and exclude monitoring costs. The coal-scrubber comparison is a crude back-of-envelope.
Endline outcomes (baler use, yields, trust) are self-reported by phone, with ~5pp differential attrition between treatment and control; Lee bounds address attrition but not experimenter-demand bias.

Internal inconsistencies: Table 5 means and coefficients do not match Table 3 and outcome labels conflict ('Burned' vs not burned); the Table 6 note mis-describes the ratio; Table A.1 says counts but shows shares; Appendix D's first page is blank.

External validity and scalability are limited: one season, two districts, screened cooperative-member burners, NGO implementer, farmer-initiated in-person monitoring; no evidence on spillovers, dynamic or strategic responses, equipment-price general-equilibrium effects, or air quality.
Arm-level comparisons (₹800 vs ₹1600 standard; 25% vs 50% upfront) are underpowered, so claims about upfront outperforming the higher payment level are descriptive.
No replication data or code are referenced, and the remote-sensing pipeline is documented only in a companion paper, limiting reproducibility.

papers.title: The Long-Run Effects of Psychotherapy on Depression Beliefs and Economic Outcomes

human_issues.text: The main pooled result (0.15 SD lower PHQ-9 scores, p = 0.08) is the finding the evaluator is least confident in. They argue that p-values between .05 and .1 are less reliable, especially for novel or surprising effects, and that such results often fail to replicate or shrink substantially.
human_issues.quote: This is the result I'm least confident in and most interested in seeing replicated.

human_issues.text: The evaluator asks for reliability evidence for the PHQ-9 outcome measure, such as Cronbach's alpha, and notes that it is hard to judge how robust each measure is from the write-up, especially for symptom subscales built from few items.
human_issues.quote: Would be nice to see Cronbach's alphas or similar for PHQ-9.

human_issues.text: The study is likely underpowered for gender differences, and the population (pregnant women and a more general population) limits generalisability, so this is a gap for future work.
human_issues.quote: I imagine the authors would be underpowered to test for gender differences given women are more widely surveyed across two interventions.

human_issues.text: Population characteristics are described too briefly. Beyond the tables, the evaluator cannot get a sense of participants' socioeconomic characteristics such as income.
human_issues.quote: I found it difficult to get a sense of population characteristics beyond what is in the tables, which was brief - e.g. a sense of income?

human_issues.text: Tasks with no clear external standard, such as relative positioning against others, are weak benchmarks for depressive realism. The evaluator also argues that self-relevant tasks confound self-perception with perceptions of others or the environment.
human_issues.quote: Tasks where there is no clear standard for reality, such as relative positioning to others, are a weak benchmark

human_issues.text: The authors conclude that the null effect on economic outcomes is explained by the sample being mostly women and social norms limiting female labor force participation; the evaluator notes this leaves open that therapy affects men's economic outcomes, which is untested. A male subsample (roughly 70 men in HAP follow-up) could be large enough to test an interaction effect.
human_issues.quote: This leaves open the possibility that therapy affects economic outcomes for men, which is not tested.

human_issues.text: Inconsistency between Figure 4's time reference ('time after enrollment') and the text in Section 5, which says the time horizon is calculated from completion of treatment, suggests a possible typo or mislabeling.
human_issues.quote: One possible typo: Figure 4 refers to "time after enrollment", while Section 5 in the text states that the time horizon is calculated from the completion of treatment.

model_issues.text: The pooled depression effect is marginal (0.15 SD, p=0.08) and driven entirely by HAP; abstract framing mixes pooled remission effects with HAP-only cost-effectiveness.
Attrition of 21% (HAP) and 31% (THPP), with more treatment-arm refusals in HAP; no Lee bounds or IPW robustness for key outcomes.

The '9 months averted' and '$7.33 per month' figures rely on linear interpolation across 3, 12 and 60 months with no uncertainty intervals; describing the cost as 'at most' is misleading given sampling error.

Preference effects (patience, altruism) are driven by unincentivized self-assessments while incentivized measures are null; demand or self-presentation effects are plausible, especially as THPP shows similar effects without depression change.
The overconfidence outcome was switched from the pre-registered initial measure to final overconfidence; the asymmetry effect is only p=0.08 (q=0.16) and insignificant in the cleanest sample.
Belief-task data quality is weak (44% non-updates, 18% wrong-direction updates, 68% with at least one irrational update), raising comprehension and noise concerns in a low-numeracy population.
Treatment reduces βH, moving updating further from the Bayesian benchmark; labelling this 'more accurate' self-assessment is partly framing.
The expert-forecast comparison on updating asymmetry is partly mechanical because the elicitation scale excluded negative ratios.
Mediation analyses (BADS, PHQ-9) lack identification of mediator effects; contemporaneous self-reported mediators cannot support causal channel claims.
The gender-norms explanation for labor and consumption nulls is untested; consumption and earnings estimates are imprecise and no male-subsample analysis is shown.
Treatment-efficacy belief elicitation was added after launch and not pre-registered, with a smaller sample (N=450).
Minor inconsistencies (775 vs 773 participants, PHQ-9 range stated as 0–21, Figure A.5 panel labels); no replication package mentioned.
